title: IBM’s ‘true ROI’ comment hits shares, exposing ETF risks
detail:
IBM’s ‘true ROI’ comment hits shares, exposing ETF risks
Opeyemi Babalola
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 11:33 AM MST 6 min read
IBM
Trade IBM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Plenty of investors own International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) without ever buying a share. The 115-year-old company sits near the top of several tech dividend, Dow dividend and even quantum computing funds.

That hidden exposure got tested on Thursday, October 22, 2026. IBM beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates, yet its shares fell about 7% in morning trading, according to 24/7 Wall St. The trigger was not the numbers but one remark about how customers judge their AI bills.

On the earnings call, CEO Arvind Krishna said big enterprises now weigh the "true ROI" of their AI spending. He added that some worry the spending could run out of control without a real payoff. Investors heard customers reaching for the brakes.

Also read: IBM spent $11 billion on growth as its own software stalls

Those nerves trace back to July, when IBM suffered the worst single-day drop in its history, falling about 25%. Big deals slipped, and analysts said clients were redirecting budgets elsewhere, including servers and memory.

A handful of funds carry most of the IBM risk

About 557 ETFs hold IBM, according to Seeking Alpha, but most own only a sliver. The real exposure sits in a short list of income and quantum funds.

The First Trust NASDAQ Technology Dividend Index Fund (TDIV) had 8.65% of its assets in IBM as of October 21, according to First Trust. At that weight, a 7% slide in IBM trims roughly six-tenths of a point from the fund if nothing else moves. That stings, but it does not break a portfolio.

Quantum funds are the stranger case. The WisdomTree Quantum Computing Fund (WQTM) and Corgi Quantum Computing ETF (CQTM) both list IBM in their top 10, according to WisdomTree and Investing.com. People bought those funds for a moonshot, and on Thursday, they got a lesson in corporate IT budgets instead.

I think that overlap is the exposure most fund owners miss. A dividend ETF and a quantum ETF can quietly stack up a large IBM position, and both just reacted to the same sentence.

Fund owners can run these checks before reacting

Start with the fund's own holdings page, since weights move daily and lists differ by source. TDIV also rebalances quarterly and caps single stocks, according to its prospectus, so an outsized IBM weight gets trimmed on schedule.

Then weigh concentration. The Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF (VYM) had under 1% in IBM, which means less risk and a smaller rebound.

None of this calls for a quick trade. It does depend on what Krishna's sentence actually meant.

IBM now expects full-year free cash flow to grow by more than $1 billion, even as shares slid on CEO Arvind Krishna's AI spending remarks.NurPhoto / Getty Images

Western Digital Corporation WDC reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 non-GAAP earnings of $4.64 per share, which surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.09. The bottom line increased 161% year over year and 30% sequentially, exceeding the high end of management's guidance of $4 (+/- 15 cents).

The company reported quarterly revenue of $4.38 billion, up 55% year over year and 17% sequentially on the back of robust customer demand and favorable pricing trends. The figure beat the consensus mark of $4.16 billion.

Western Digital Corporation Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise
Western Digital Corporation Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Western Digital Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Western Digital Corporation Quote

Western Digital shipped 248 exabytes in the quarter, up 22% year over year and 8% sequentially. Nearline products remained the primary growth driver as the company advanced its product transitions. WDC is ramping up its latest-generation ePMR drives, with capacities up to 40TB, and plans to introduce HAMR technology in the first half of calendar 2027. These developments are expected to support stronger year-over-year growth in exabyte shipments. Adoption is advancing faster than in previous technology transitions, with WDC expecting the new platform to account for nearly 30% of nearline shipments in the fiscal second quarter and 50% in the fiscal third quarter of 2027.

Western Digital's board of directors declared a quarterly cash dividend of 17.5 cents per share, representing a 17% increase from the previous dividend, payable on Dec. 17, 2026, to shareholders of record as of Dec. 4, 2026. The dividend increase highlights the company's financial momentum and its commitment to returning capital to shareholders.

In the past year, shares have gained 173.6% compared with the Zacks Computer-Storage Devices industry's rise of 178.4%.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Quarter in Detail

Cloud end market revenue reached $3.9 billion (88% of total revenue), rising 54% year over year. Growth was driven by sustained demand for high-capacity nearline HDDs, including the initial ramp-up of its latest ePMR platform. Strong pricing trends further reflect the value and total cost of ownership (TCO) benefits the company offers its customers.

Revenues from the Client end market (7%) were up 119% year over year to $320 million.

Revenues from the Consumer end market (5%) surged 19% year over year to $193 million.

Margins

Non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 58.1%, up 1,420 basis points (bps) year over year with incremental gross margin exceeding 80%. A favorable mix of higher-capacity drives, disciplined operational execution and stronger pricing across its portfolio drove the improvement. The company also reported a 28% year-over-year increase in average price per terabyte, accelerating from the high-teens growth recorded in the previous quarter.

IBM just reported Q3 2026 and the headline is simple. Revenue landed at US$17.1b and basic earnings per share came in at US$2.33, while operating pretax margin widened by 70 basis points. The twist is in the mood, not the math. After a 17.7% gain over the past three months, the stock barely moved today, up only 0.3%. title: What Is The Biggest Threat To Accenture Stock?
detail:
What Is The Biggest Threat To Accenture Stock?

Accenture (ACN) stock returned 77.4% over the three months to October 22, 2026, against 3.7% for the S&P 500. Such a run leaves shareholders with more to lose, and one remark from the October 1 earnings call merits their attention: management discussed what Accenture can charge its clients. So what did management say about prices, and how much of Accenture's revenue is at stake?

Accenture Saw Lower Pricing In Many Areas

Management said on the October 1 call that Accenture saw lower pricing in many areas of its business in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended August 31. Pricing was overall stable for the full year, and management described the market as highly competitive. So the shift is a recent, one-quarter development rather than a yearlong trend.

Management also discussed AI on the call. Accenture is delivering more AI efficiencies to clients, management said, and has more than made up for that with new kinds of work and broader scope.

Hiring patterns reflect the same shift. Revenue per person rose in fiscal 2026, and management expects to hire at a lower rate in fiscal 2027, in part due to AI. That outlines the threat in plain terms: if AI lets Accenture do the same work with fewer people, clients may expect to pay less for it, and so far management has found new work to fill the gap.

How Much Of Accenture's Revenue Is Exposed?

Management did not say how much revenue saw lower pricing. The pressure applies to a business with $74.2 billion in revenue over the twelve months ended August 31, 2026, up 6.5% in U.S. dollars from a year earlier. Consulting revenues were $36.9 billion in fiscal 2026, up 3% in local currency, the slower of the two halves of that revenue. Managed services revenues, derived from running applications, infrastructure and operations for clients, were $37.3 billion, up 6% in local currency.

The company's outlook leaves room for a weaker year. Management expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 3% to 6% in local currency, against 5% in fiscal 2026, and expects acquisitions to add 2% to 2.5% of that. The bottom of the range allows for deterioration, management said.

The share price leaves less room than it did in the summer. On June 30, 2026, the stock traded at 9.8 times earnings, its lowest multiple at any of the 40 quarter ends since fiscal 2017. It now trades at 18.6 times earnings, against 23.0 for the S&P 500, and its latest close was 7.7% below its highest close of the past year. The current price appears to assume that lower pricing stays contained.

title: IBM's Software Growth Sped Up and Its Stock Barely Moved. I'd Start Buying.
detail:
IBM's Software Growth Sped Up and Its Stock Barely Moved. I'd Start Buying.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:01 AM MST 5 min read
IBM
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Before International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) posted third-quarter results on Oct. 21, I set a bar for buying the stock. I wanted software revenue growth back in the high single digits and recurring revenue rising close to 10%.

The software half of that test came through. IBM's software segment reported 9% year-over-year revenue growth at constant currency (a measure that strips out exchange-rate moves). In the second quarter, it grew just 5%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But shares barely budged on Thursday, the day after the report, closing up less than 1% after falling as much as 4% during the session. IBM stock closed at $252.11, which puts it about 23% under the $329.23 record close it set on June 2.

In September, I wrote that I expected IBM stock to be higher in five years but still wouldn't buy it. What I was waiting for was software growth that picked back up. I think this quarter delivered it.

Image source: Getty Images.

Software is growing faster again

Software matters more to IBM's profits than any other piece of the business. The segment made up around 46% of third-quarter revenue but about 65% of the company's segment profit, so its swing this year counts for a lot.

Software's constant-currency growth was 8% in the first quarter of 2026. It cooled to 5% in the second quarter before jumping to 9% in the third -- its fastest rate of the year. Transaction processing, the software linked largely to IBM's mainframes, did most of the swinging. It dropped 9% at constant currency in the second quarter and climbed 10% in the third. Better still, software's segment profit rose 15% year over year to around $2.7 billion, and its margin widened to 35% from 33%.

"Software revenue growth accelerated four points sequentially to 9% this quarter, including over four points of organic growth," chief financial officer Jim Kavanaugh said on IBM's Oct. 21 earnings call.

Granted, some of the jump is timing. Kavanaugh said around a quarter of the acceleration came from big deals that slipped out of the second quarter and closed in the third. The other three-quarters, he said, came from new business.

I think this makes the second quarter look like the exception, not the start of a slide.

Does the unchanged revenue forecast matter?

IBM still expects full-year revenue to climb 4% to 5% at constant currency, the same range it set in July. But it now expects 2026 free cash flow to rise by over $1 billion from last year's $14.7 billion. In July, it expected a gain of around $1 billion.

Rigetti Computing (RGTI) stock fell 68.2% in the year to October 22, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned 15.7%. The company's sales grew over that year, so the fall has more to do with what investors will pay for those sales than with the sales themselves. News reports on October 23, 2025, put the stock's one-year run at more than 5,500%, and its highest close of the past year, $44.27, came on October 31, 2025. So how much less are investors now paying for each dollar of Rigetti's sales?

Rigetti Stock Costs Far Less Per Dollar Of Sales

At the end of September 2025, three weeks before the one-year window above opens, investors paid 1,292 times Rigetti's trailing twelve-month sales for the stock. At the October 22, 2026 close, they paid 286.5 times. The business did not shrink over that stretch: revenue for the twelve months to June 2026 rose 68.5% from a year earlier to $13.4 million.

Other quantum stocks lost favor too. IonQ, another quantum computing company, fell 44% over the same year, and D-Wave Quantum fell 57%. Rigetti fell further than both. Even after the drop, Rigetti's multiple of 286.5 times is far above the 3.1 times sales the S&P 500 trades at.

What Rigetti Reported And Announced Over Twelve Months

On January 9, 2026, the company pushed back the date for general availability of its 108-qubit system, Cepheus-1-108Q. Fourth-quarter 2025 revenue of $1.87 million then came in below the $2.37 million analysts expected. News reports on March 5, 2026, said the miss sent the shares 9% lower in early trading, and the stock closed the day down 4.4%.

On May 21, 2026, Rigetti announced a letter of intent under which the Department of Commerce selected it for up to $100 million in funding over three years, and the shares rose 30.6% that day. In September 2026, Rigetti announced a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce, yet the stock closed at its lowest level of the past year on October 22.

Second-quarter 2026 revenue rose 185.3% from a year earlier to $5.14 million. Management said on the August 6, 2026 call that the increase came from on-premises Novera QPU sales. Rigetti also has an $8.4 million C-DAC order for a 108-qubit system in India, which management expects to recognize in the fourth quarter of 2026. That single order is worth more than all of Rigetti's second-quarter revenue. Management said its revenue continues to be influenced by the timing of system deliveries and government-funded projects.

title: Why Isn't IBM's Stock Bouncing Back After Strong Earnings Results?
detail:
Why Isn't IBM's Stock Bouncing Back After Strong Earnings Results?
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 11:17 AM MST 4 min read
IBM
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

In July, IBM (NYSE:IBM) stock suffered the worst day in its 115-year history, falling about 25% after the company warned that customers had shifted spending away from its products.

The miss was clearly a matter of timing -- a series of major contracts IBM was planning didn't close by the end of the quarter, as its customers shifted spending to memory and storage products whose prices were increasing rapidly.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Three months later, IBM's third-quarter report, which landed on Oct. 21, mostly backed that assessment up, and the company posted strong revenue and earnings. So, why isn't the stock bouncing back?

Image source: Getty Images.

The good news was real

IBM's revenue rose 5% to $17.1 billion in the third quarter, up from 1% growth in the second. Software grew 9% at constant currency, and operating earnings per share rose 11% to $2.95. Free cash flow was $3 billion, and management raised its full-year outlook to FCF growth of more than $1 billion.

CFO Jim Kavanaugh said about two-thirds of the large software deals that slipped in the second quarter closed in the third. Transaction processing software, which is tied to mainframes, swung from a 9% decline to 10% growth. That looks like delayed spending, not lost customers.

Some of that growth was bought

IBM closed its roughly $11 billion acquisition of Confluent in March, so that revenue wasn't included in last year's numbers. Confluent's last reported quarterly revenue was $314.8 million, and IBM's software revenue in Q3 2025 was $7.2 billion. So that would put IBM's organic software growth in this quarter at around 4%. That's real progress, but it's less dramatic than 9%.

Management is also tapping the brakes. CEO Arvind Krishna said he doesn't expect transaction processing to keep growing at double digits, and IBM expects that business to be flat for the year. Kavanaugh said the company is expecting about $32 billion in full-year software revenue. Subtract the $22.6 billion IBM has recognized through nine months, and the fourth quarter works out to roughly 4% growth, versus 8% in the third. Mainframe hardware sales also fell 20%, although that came against a very strong launch a year ago.

IBM is a long-term buy

I still like IBM as a long-term investment in AI and quantum computing, but I'm not ignoring the risks. IBM spent $11.4 billion on acquisitions this year, so cash fell $3.4 billion to $11.1 billion, and debt rose $2.6 billion to $63.8 billion. The dividend looks well covered -- IBM paid $4.8 billion of dividends against $7.8 billion of free cash flow through nine months -- but there's less cushion for another big deal. Meanwhile, shareholders receive a dividend yield of about 2.7%.
